paragraphs: Where was he running? “Where else could she be but at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s? She must have gone straight to him from Samsonov’s. That was clear now. The whole intrigue, the whole deceit, was plain as day.” ... It all went whirling through his head. He did not run to Marya Kondratyevna’s. “No need to go there ... not the slightest need ... he must not raise an alarm ... they would run and tell on him right away.... Marya Kondratyevna was clearly in the plot, and Smerdyakov too, yes, he too, they had all been bought!”

He settled on a different plan. He went a long way around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, crossed the lane, ran down Dmitrovsky Street and over the little bridge, and came out at the deserted alley behind the house, which was empty and uninhabited. On one side was the wattle fence of a neighbor’s kitchen-garden. On the other was the tall, strong fence that ran all around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. Here he chose a spot, apparently the very one where, as the story went and he knew it, Lizaveta had once climbed over. “If she could climb over it,” the thought came to him, God knows why, “surely I can.” He jumped up and at once got a grip on the top of the fence. Then he hauled himself up with all his strength and sat astride it. The bath-house stood close by in the garden, but from the fence he could also see the lit windows of the house.

“Yes, the old man’s bedroom is lit up. She’s there!” And he leapt down from the fence into the garden. He knew Grigory was ill, and probably Smerdyakov too, and that nobody could hear him. Even so, he hid by instinct, stood stock-still and listened. But all around was dead silence, and, as if arranged on purpose, perfect stillness. Not the slightest breath of wind.

“And naught but the whispering silence,” a line of verse rose in his mind, he did not know why. “If only nobody heard me jump the fence! I don’t think they did.” He stood still for a minute. Then he walked softly across the grass of the garden, keeping clear of the trees and shrubs. He went slowly, creeping on tiptoe at every step, listening to the sound of his own feet. It took him five minutes to get to the lighted window. He remembered that directly under the window there were several thick, tall bushes of elder and whitebeam. The door from the house into the garden, on the left side, was shut. He had looked carefully to make sure of that as he passed. At last he reached the bushes and hid behind them. He held his breath. “Now I must wait,” he thought, “so they settle down, in case they heard my steps and are listening ... if only I don’t cough or sneeze.”

He waited two minutes. His heart was pounding, and at times he could barely breathe. “No, this thumping won’t stop,” he thought. “I can’t wait any longer.” He stood behind a bush, in its shadow. The window’s light lay across the front of the bush.

“How red the whitebeam berries are!” he murmured, not knowing why. Softly and silently, step by step, he came up to the window and rose on tiptoe. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s whole bedroom lay open to his eyes. It was a smallish room, split in two by a red screen, “Chinese,” as Fyodor Pavlovitch liked to call it. The word “Chinese” flashed through Mitya’s mind, “and behind the screen is Grushenka,” thought Mitya. He began to study Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had on a new striped-silk dressing-gown that Mitya had never seen, tied with a silk cord with tassels. Under the collar of the gown peeped a clean, dandyish shirt of fine linen with gold studs. On his head Fyodor Pavlovitch wore the same red bandage Alyosha had seen.
“So he’s dolled himself up,” thought Mitya.

His father stood near the window, seemingly lost in thought. All at once he jerked his head up and listened for a moment. Hearing nothing, he went over to the table and poured himself half a glass of brandy from a decanter, which he drank off. Then he gave a deep sigh and stood a moment more. He strolled to the looking-glass on the wall, lifted the red bandage a little from his forehead with his right hand, and started inspecting his bruises and scars, which had not yet healed.
“He’s alone,” thought Mitya. “Most likely he’s alone.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch stepped away from the looking-glass, turned abruptly toward the window and looked out. Mitya slid back into the shadow at once.

“She may be there behind the screen. Perhaps she’s asleep by now,” he thought, with a stab at his heart. Fyodor Pavlovitch left the window. “He was looking out for her, so she isn’t there. Why else would he peer into the dark? He’s wild with impatience.” ... Mitya crept forward again at once and went back to gazing in at the window. The old man had sat down at the table, looking disappointed. At last he rested his elbow on the table and leaned his right cheek on his hand. Mitya watched him greedily.
“He’s alone, he’s alone!” he said again. “If she were here, his face would be different.”

Oddly enough, a strange, senseless annoyance rose in him that she was not here. “It’s not that she isn’t here,” he explained to himself immediately, “it’s that I can’t tell for certain whether she is or not.” Mitya remembered afterward that his mind was unusually clear at that moment and that he took in everything, down to the least detail, and missed nothing. But a feeling of misery, the misery of uncertainty and indecision, was growing in his heart with every instant. “Is she here or not?” The angry doubt filled him, and suddenly, making up his mind, he reached out and knocked softly on the window frame. He knocked the signal the old man had agreed on with Smerdyakov: two slow knocks, then three quicker ones, the signal that meant “Grushenka is here!”
The old man gave a start, jerked up his head, sprang to his feet and ran to the window. Mitya slid away into the shadow. Fyodor Pavlovitch opened the window and stuck his whole head out.
“Grushenka, is that you? Is it you?” he said, in a kind of shaky half-whisper. “Where are you, my angel, where are you?” He was dreadfully excited and gasping for breath.
“He’s alone.” That settled it for Mitya.

“Where are you?” the old man cried again. He pushed his head out farther, right out to the shoulders, staring in every direction, left and right. “Come here, I’ve a little present for you. Come, I’ll show you....”
“He means the three thousand,” thought Mitya.
“But where are you? Are you at the door? I’ll open it this minute.”

And the old man all but climbed out of the window, peering to the right, where a door led into the garden, trying to see through the darkness. One second more and he would surely have run out to open the door, without waiting for Grushenka to answer.

Mitya watched him from the side without moving. He hated that profile so: the dangling Adam’s apple, the hooked nose, the lips smiling in greedy expectation. All of it stood out brightly in the slanting lamplight falling from the room on the left. A horrible fury of hatred suddenly swept through Mitya: “There he was, his rival, the man who had tormented him and wrecked his life!” It was a surge of that sudden, furious, vengeful rage which he had described to Alyosha, almost as if he had foreseen it, four days before in the arbor. Alyosha had asked him, “How can you say you’ll kill our father?” and he had answered, “I don’t know, I don’t know. Perhaps I shall not kill him, perhaps I shall. I’m afraid he’ll suddenly be so loathsome to me at that moment. I hate his double chin, his nose, his eyes, his shameless grin. I feel a personal repulsion. That’s what I’m afraid of, that’s what may be too much for me.” ... That personal repulsion was becoming unbearable. Mitya lost all control. Suddenly he pulled the brass pestle out of his pocket.

“God was watching over me then,” Mitya himself said later. At that very moment Grigory woke on his sickbed. Earlier that evening he had gone through the treatment Smerdyakov had described to Ivan. He had rubbed himself all over with vodka mixed with a secret, very strong brew, and had drunk what was left of it while his wife said a “certain prayer” over him. Then he had gone to bed. Marfa Ignatyevna had tasted the stuff too. Not being used to strong drink, she slept like the dead beside her husband.

But Grigory woke in the middle of the night, quite suddenly. He thought for a moment, and though a sharp pain shot through his back at once, he sat up in bed. Then he thought again, got up and dressed in a hurry. Perhaps his conscience pricked him at the idea of sleeping while the house stood unguarded “in such perilous times.” Smerdyakov, worn out by his fit, lay motionless in the next room. Marfa Ignatyevna did not stir. “The stuff’s been too much for the woman,” Grigory thought, glancing at her, and with a groan he went out onto the steps. He surely meant only to look around from the steps, for he could hardly walk. The pain in his back and in his right leg was unbearable. But all at once he remembered that he had not locked the little garden gate that evening. He was the most punctual and exact of men, a man who held to a fixed routine and to habits of many years. Limping and twisting with pain, he went down the steps and toward the garden. Yes, the gate was standing wide open. He stepped into the garden without thinking. Maybe he imagined something, maybe he heard a sound. He glanced to the left and saw his master’s window open. Nobody was looking out of it just then.

“Why is it open? It’s not summer,” thought Grigory. And at that very instant he glimpsed something extraordinary ahead of him in the garden. Forty paces off, a man seemed to be running through the dark. Some kind of shadow was moving very fast.

“Good Lord!” cried Grigory, beside himself. Forgetting the pain in his back, he hurried to cut off the running figure. He took a short cut, evidently knowing the garden better. The figure in flight made for the bath-house, ran around behind it and dashed to the garden fence. Grigory followed, never losing sight of him, and ran, forgetting everything. He reached the fence just as the man was climbing over. Grigory cried out in a frenzy, pounced on him and seized his leg in both hands.
Yes, his foreboding had not deceived him. He knew him. It was he, the “monster,” the “parricide.”
“Parricide!” the old man shouted so loudly that the whole neighborhood could have heard. But he had no time to shout more. He dropped at once, as if struck by lightning.

Mitya jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. He had the brass pestle in his hand, and he flung it away mechanically into the grass. It landed two paces from Grigory, not in the grass but on the path, in a very conspicuous place. For some seconds he stared at the figure stretched out before him. The old man’s head was covered in blood. Mitya reached out and began to feel it. Afterward he remembered clearly how desperately anxious he had been to find out whether he had smashed the old man’s skull or only stunned him with the pestle. But the blood was pouring out horribly, and in a moment Mitya’s fingers were drenched in the hot stream. He remembered pulling out of his pocket the clean white handkerchief he had put there for his visit to Madame Hohlakov and pressing it to the old man’s head, senselessly trying to wipe the blood off his face and temples. But the handkerchief was soaked with blood in an instant.

“Good heavens! What am I doing this for?” thought Mitya, suddenly pulling himself together. “If I’ve smashed his skull, how can I find out now? And what difference does it make now?” he added, hopelessly. “If I’ve killed him, I’ve killed him.... You’ve come to grief, old man, so there you must lie!” he said aloud. And turning suddenly to the fence, he vaulted over it into the lane and ran—he clutched the blood-soaked handkerchief crushed in his right fist, and as he ran he shoved it into the back pocket of his coat. He ran headlong. The few people who passed him in the dark streets remembered afterward that they had met a man running that night. He flew back to the widow Morozov’s house.

As soon as he had left it that evening, Fenya had rushed to the head porter, Nazar Ivanovitch, and begged him, for Christ’s sake, “not to let the captain in again today or tomorrow.” Nazar Ivanovitch promised. But then his mistress suddenly sent for him, and he went upstairs. On the way he met his nephew, a boy of twenty who had only lately come from the country, and told him to take his place, but forgot to mention “the captain.” Mitya ran up to the gate and knocked. The lad knew him at once, for Mitya had tipped him more than once. He opened the gate right away, let him in, and hurried to tell him, with a cheerful smile, that “Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t at home now, you know.”
“Where is she, then, Prohor?” asked Mitya, stopping short.
“She set off this evening, about two hours ago, with Timofey, for Mokroe.”
“What for?” cried Mitya.
“That I can’t say. To see some officer. Somebody invited her, and they sent horses to fetch her.”
Mitya left him and ran like a madman to Fenya.
